"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently," she said.

Chiang said she has "serious concerns" about how those standards were applied in her case, and she said those concerns "deserve to be taken seriously."

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard," she said. "That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

Chiang's statement doesn't spell out the specific nature surrounding her departure from Xbox, so many will naturally want more answers. Those could come in time, as Chiang said this is "not the whole story."

Another former Xbox executive, Shannon Loftis, commented on Chiang's post to say she is "Team Helen all the way." Loftis said she wonders who may have leaked the "false information" about Chiang and what their motivations may have been. In any event, she says it shows a "loss of moral character and 'clarity' in leadership at Xbox."

"A real leadership team would have relentlessly pursued the 'leaker' and taken appropriate action because 'confidential personnel matters' actually are bases for defamation lawsuits," she said. "It's a clownshow up in there and I feel terrible for anyone that still has to deal with it."

A spokesperson for Microsoft told Windows Central that the company does not “discuss individual personnel matters.”

According to a source speaking to Eurogamer, Chiang was “terminated for policy violations.” The Verge’s Tom Warren backed this up, saying Chiang was cut loose due to a “policy violation,” but the exact nature of that is unknown.

In July, Sharma announced that Chiang would become Xbox’s first-ever COO, with “end-to-end” responsibility for the financial future of Xbox’s content, hardware, platform, and services.

Chiang had worked at Microsoft for 20 years, in that time playing a key role in the creation of Xbox Live and later shepherding Mojang and the lucrative Minecraft franchise. As COO, Chiang was expected to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results,” Sharma said.

For her part, Sharma said she will have an update to share on the COO position at Xbox at some point, but she didn’t divulge more.

The Xbox business was “not healthy” when Sharma took over, she said, and Chiang no doubt had a challenging road ahead of her. As for now, however, people can only speculate as to the real reason she left Xbox.

title: All Call of Duty Games In Order
summary:
Call of Duty is a household name for first-person shooters, and Activision has released yearly titles for over two decades. Some entries of the franchise were obscure and platform-specific games, but most Call of Duty titles have been major fall releases across multiple platforms.

The first few Call of Duty games focused on World War II and authenticity as a military shooter, but over the years the franchise has grown in complexity and often leaned away from a mil-sim design. Call of Duty has evolved with third game modes, robots, spaceships, jetpacks, and sometimes mind-bending fictional campaigns that steer more toward sci-fi and fantasy than the game's initial military roots.

The first Call of Duty game was developed by Infinity Ward, but today's current games are a collaborative effort across multiple Call of Duty studios: Treyarch, Raven Software, Infinity Ward, Sledgehammer Games, Beenox, Demonware, High Moon Studios, and more.

Below we list all of the Call of Duty games in order of release.

Call of Duty

The very first Call of Duty was originally a PC game released in 2003, but an enhanced port titled Call of Duty: Classic was later developed by a separate studio and released worldwide in November 2009.

Developed by Infinity Ward, Call of Duty put players in the shoes of three infantry soldiers in World War II. This single-player campaign was squad-based, pairing the player with AI-teammates for missions featuring the American, British, and Soviet forces.

Call of Duty 2

Call of Duty 2: Big Red One

In 2005, a second Call of Duty game was released, and this was the first title developed by Treyarch. Call of Duty 2: Big Red One was available for GameCube, Xbox One, and PlayStation 2.

This was another first-person military shooter set during World War II, but it differed from the previous Call of Duty campaigns because Big Red One only featured one protagonist, with the storyline focusing on a single soldier from the American 1st Infantry Division. This division is historically known as the "Big Red One" and became the most recognized U.S. Army formation of World War II. The campaign missions covered the division's part in North Africa, the invasion of Sicily, storming the beaches of Normandy on D-Day, and eventually the push into Germany.

Treyarch also developed 2006's Call of Duty 3, and it was released for PlayStation 2, Xbox, Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and Wii. This sequel kept Call of Duty rooted in World War II, but instead of featuring a campaign that focused on several parts of the war, Treyarch centered the game on the 1944 Battle of Normandy. Call of Duty 3 introduced the series to QTEs (quick-time-events) and featured more close-quarters combat than the previous games.

This was the only Call of Duty ever made for the PSP, and like all the Call of Duty games before it, focused on the stories of World War II. The story included American, Canadian, and British campaign missions.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare

Call of Duty's original creator, Infinity Ward, returned to develop 2007's Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. This entry finally pulled Call of Duty out of the World War II cycle, and this fourth main installment marked the first modern setting of the franchise. Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was an award-winning title, and it featured a single-player campaign that allowed players to bounce between perspectives of the U.S. Marines and the British S.A.S. in a modern war story against a global threat of a rogue enemy faction. This campaign also introduced iconic characters who would later become household names in the series, with Captain Price, "Soap" MacTavish, and Gaz.

A remastered version of Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was later developed by Raven Software and titled Call of Duty: Modern Warfare Remastered. This version was released as part of special edition bundles of Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare in 2016 and as a standalone version became available in 2017.

Developed by Treyarch, Call of Duty: World at War was available for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, PC, and Wii. This was the first Call of Duty to feature a cooperative campaign, and it could be played split-screen or online co-op.

Call of Duty: World at War's campaign focused on the Pacific and Eastern Front theaters of World War II, with missions featuring the perspectives of US Marine Private C. Miller and the Soviet Red Army's Private Dimitri Petrenko. The story is a prequel for what would become Treyarch's popular Call of Duty: Black Ops series.

World at War is also notable for being the introduction of Call of Duty's Zombies mode. Originally, players needed to beat the final campaign mission to unlock the Zombies mode with the Nacht der Untoten map. Post-launch DLC packs added additional Zombies maps, and eventually players no longer needed to beat the campaign to unlock access to the mode.

The game's campaign followed Task Force 141, a new multinational special forces unit commanded by Modern Warfare's Captain "Soap" MacTavish. Captain Price also returned, and the new task force introduced one of Call of Duty's most beloved and recognizable characters of the franchise with Simon "Ghost" Riley, who wears the iconic ghost face mask.

The campaign features one of Call of Duty's most infamous antagonists, Vladimir Makarov. The game also created a lot of controversy, as Modern Warfare 2 contained a campaign mission where the player participated in Makarov's extreme terrorist attack on an airport.

Additionally, it's worth noting that Modern Warfare 2 also introduced a third game mode to Call of Duty with Spec Ops. MW2 Spec Ops mode featured twenty-three additional campaign-style missions that could be played individually or cooperatively with a teammate. Each mission had three tiers of difficulty. These Spec Ops missions gained enough praise and popularity to return the mode in later Call of Duty games.

Even now, Call of Duty: Black Ops still stands out as one of the franchise's most mind-bending and mystery-driven storylines. The campaign was set in the 1960s during the Cold War, and it followed CIA operative Alex Mason as he attempted to recall specific memories. The story required the player to work through the missions to uncover the meaning of a mysterious set of numbers. Black Ops 1 also introduced some of the most iconic characters of the franchise, with Frank Woods and Jason Hudson assisting Mason throughout the campaign.

It's also worth noting that Treyarch's Zombies mode from World at War returned in Black Ops. The mode featured more complex maps and an in-depth storyline with Easter eggs for players to solve. Black Ops also introduced the first version of Treyarch's popular Dead Ops Arcade, which was an unlockable retro-style, twin-stick shooter variant of Zombies mode.

Despite ending on a cliffhanger, Call of Duty: Ghosts has remained a standalone title in the franchise. The game took place in a future setting where the United States was a war-torn area with a weakened government. The game's main protagonists were the Ghosts, a force of U.S. Special Operations soldiers. The story centered around two brothers, their father, and a dog named Riley, who the player could instruct and use as a means of recon and stealth attacks on various missions.

Ghosts introduced a brand-new third game mode called Extinction. This was a 4-player co-op survival mode similar to Zombies, but the mode was themed around an alien invasion. The story followed a soldier named Jack Mitchell, who joined a resistance fighting against a private military corporation that became a global threat.

Beating Black Ops 3's campaign unlocked a Nightmare mode, where the entire story could be experienced with the addition of zombies and Zombie-mode features. The game also featured a full Zombies mode experience with new maps.

Infinite Warfare also featured a Zombies mode that wasn't developed by Treyarch. Infinity Ward's take on the mode included a more cartoony art style and paid homage to movie genres across various time periods.

Taking Call of Duty back to its roots, WW2 centered around a squad in the US's 1st Infantry Division. The story followed their battles on the Western Front, and it mainly covered the historical events around D-Day. The game also included another Zombies mode by Sledgehammer Games, but this time the mode was geared more towards horror and gore with a Nazi Zombies theme.

The game was released on PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and PC, and the story centered around a rebooted version of the original cast, with the return of Captain Price, Soap MacTavish, and Gaz. It also introduced new characters who became notable in this new series, including Farah Karim, Alex Keller, and Kate Laswell. Together the cast worked to help the fictional country of Urzikstan hold off a Russian invasion.

Warzone's Verdansk map featured POIs from Modern Warfare 2019, and it included the game's operators, weapons, and equipment. The battle royale's arrival felt perfectly timed, as it was released during the start of the pandemic, and it featured a free-to-play model that allowed everyone to squad up while they practiced social distancing.

Warzone has featured several maps and modes over the years. It remains Call of Duty's live service battle royale game, and each year since the game has been updated and integrated with Call of Duty's newest fall release. Vanguard's campaign is more character-driven and told from the perspective of multiple different WWII soldiers in a non-linear order. These characters were eventually recruited to form Task Force Vanguard and stop a secret Nazi program.

The campaign served as a direct sequel to Modern Warfare 2019, and offered a new formation of the iconic Task Force 141 from the original series. Task Force 141 teamed up with a Mexican Special Forces unit as they attempted to track down a terrorist who had gained possession of American-made ballistic missiles.

Modern Warfare 2 included a Spec Ops co-op mode, and it introduced the DMZ extraction mode to Warzone.

The story once again followed the beloved Task Force 141 as they tracked down the Russian terrorist, Vladimir Makarov, but the campaign was widely criticized for featuring open-world filler missions in between the standard story missions.

The game launched with an open-world Zombies mode developed by Treyarch, but instead of standard round-based Zombies, the mode featured an extraction-style game loop on Warzone's Urzikstan map.

Black Ops 6 was themed as a 1990s spy-thriller that followed rogue CIA operatives Troy Marshall and Frank Woods as they assembled a team of agents to hunt down Pantheon, an international paramilitary terrorist organization. It also introduced the game's first rendition of Treyarch's advanced "ominmovement" system, which lets players walk, sprint, and dive in any direction.

Black Ops 6 also featured a full Zombies mode with the return of classic round-based maps created by Treyarch.

The campaign features up to four-player co-op, and the story serves as a sequel to 2012's Black Ops 2. David Mason returns to lead an elite Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC) team on a covert mission to Call of Duty's fictional city of Avalon. It's there they uncover a weapon engineered to turn fear into an instrument of war, which presents a global threat. Additionally, this is Call of Duty's first campaign to feature "end game" content, which adds a new cooperative experience on the map of Avalon.

The game also launches with the largest round-based Zombies map ever created, which is inspired by Black Ops 2's Tranzit map.

This Call of Duty ditched the older generation of console platforms, launching only on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC, and Switch 2. This is also the first Call of Duty game featured on a Nintendo platform in over a decade.

The Modern Warfare 4 campaign featured two main storylines with intertwining narratives. This single-player experience wrapped up the rebooted Modern Warfare series' ongoing storyline featuring Captain Price and Task Force 141, as well as introduced a new cast of characters fighting through a full-scale invasion of South Korea.

This was the first Call of Duty to feature a cooperative campaign, and it could be played split-screen or online co-op.

Call of Duty: World at War's campaign focused on the Pacific and Eastern Front theaters of World War II, with missions featuring the perspectives of US Marine Private C. Miller and the Soviet Red Army's Private Dimitri Petrenko. The story is a prequel for what would become Treyarch's popular Call of Duty: Black Ops series.

World at War is also notable for being the introduction of Call of Duty's Zombies mode. Originally, players needed to beat the final campaign mission to unlock the Zombies mode with the Nacht der Untoten map. Post-launch DLC packs added additional Zombies maps, and eventually players no longer needed to beat the campaign to unlock access to the mode.

Captain Price also returned, and the new task force introduced one of Call of Duty's most beloved and recognizable characters of the franchise with Simon "Ghost" Riley, who wears the iconic ghost face mask.

title: CoD: Modern Warfare 4 Arrives To Warzone With New Maps, Movement, And Features
summary:
Season 1 of Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone arrives on November 6, and this fully integrates the new Call of Duty into battle royale. The season update replaces Black Ops 7's maps with two Modern Warfare-themed maps, overhauls Warzone's movement, introduces new game mechanics, and adds an operator-skin toggle feature. Here is everything you need to know when Season 1 of Modern Warfare 4 goes live in Warzone.

Additionally, Season 1 of Modern Warfare 4 adds a new battle pass, more multiplayer maps and modes, and plenty of new DMZ content. There are four new DLC weapons to unlock for use in MW4 and battle royale. This big update also also celebrates the launch of Warzone on the Nintendo Switch 2.

MW4 integration and level reset

Season 1 marks the start of a new year of Warzone, meaning all players will be reset to player level one. Players will have the choice to level up and prestige across multiplayer, DMZ, and Warzone. 

All of Modern Warfare 4's operators, weapons, attachments, and camos will be available to use in battle royale. However, Warzone's "legacy" weapons will work differently this year. The older guns from the last three Call of Duty games will become "legacy" weapons, and while they are still available to use, they will no longer be customizable in the Gunsmith. 

Black Ops 7's omnimovement is also removed from the game, transitioning battle royale to Modern Warfare 4's scaled-back movement with fluid sliding and mantling mechanics.

New Warzone maps

For Season 1, DMZ’s Hajin will launch as Warzone's large standard battle royale map, while Zodiac arrives as the smaller Resurgence map. All other Warzone maps will be removed from the game.

Hajin features the same points-of-interest as the DMZ version of the map, and it will also include the mode's dynamic weather with rain and fog. However, the battle royale version of the map will feature Warzone's 1v1 Gulag arena, and there will be two Gulag layouts for players to experience.

Verdansk and Rebirth Island will both return later in the season, allowing a rotation of maps for both battle royale and Resurgence modes. Black Ops 7's Avalon and the Fortune's Keep Resurgence map are not expected to return.

New Warzone features

Zipline Launcher

Season 1 adds the new Zipline Launcher, which is a device that players can use to create anchors and a zipline for traversing Warzone's various terrain. Once deployed, the Zipline Launcher will remain active on the map until it’s either retrieved or destroyed.

Grabber Drone

The Grabber Drone is a rare drone equipped with a device capable of picking up various loot, environmental objects, and even operators. Players can use this drone to pick up a downed teammate and move them closer for a revive, retrieve difficult to reach weapons and other items, and even retrieve loot from a Buy Station.

Interactive objects

This new season adds interactive objects to Warzone's map, including explosive fuel barrels, which can be picked up and placed in strategic ways. There are also several items players can move around the maps, such as dumpsters, cable spools, and construction equipment to either provide cover or block enemy pathways.

Additional gameplay adjustments

Other changes include gameplay adjustments:

  • Tactical Sprint will be available to all Operators without the need for a perk, but its duration is slightly shortened
  • Players can drag their allies while reviving them, pulling them out of harm’s way
  • Additional weapon-balance tuning
  • Improved visibility and readability across all maps
  • Improved footstep audio

Activision says more details on these new gameplay adjustments and specific weapon tuning will arrive with Warzone's Season 1 patch notes later in the week.

Warzone support ends for PS4 and Xbox One

As previously announced, Warzone will no longer be playable on PlayStation 4 and Xbox One, as Modern Warfare 4 ditches the older generation of console hardware. Players will still keep progression if they return to a supported platform and use the same linked Activision account.

Operator-skin toggle

Warzone's new operator-skin toggle feature is also arriving with Season 1. Warzone is currently filled with wacky skins and cel-shaded characters introduced in recent years, but players can toggle on a filter to remove any of these outlandish skins and replace them all with Modern Warfare 4 operators. The toggle also only impacts the user’s game, and it does not alter the experience of others. This new feature will be off by default.

title: When Is Resident Evil Coming To Home Video? It Could Be Very Soon
summary:
Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie crushed it at the box office, banking more than $400 million globally to become the most successful entry in the series ever. When will the film be available to watch at home, though?

According to Fandango, the home video release is set for November 3. That's apparently when people can buy the movie outright or rent it digitally, with a physical edition for Blu-ray coming at some point later. It will also presumably come to streaming at some point, and it should hit Netflix given the multi-billion-dollar Pay-1 deal the two companies have in place.

While we wait, Netflix just announced that director Paul W.S. Anderson's original Resident Evil, along with its follow-up, Resident Evil: Apocalypse, are now available to stream.

They join the other Resident Evil movies already on Netflix, including Resident Evil: Afterlife, Resident Evil: Retribution, Resident Evil: Extinction, and Resident Evil: The Final Chapter. The 2022 Resident Evil TV show is also currently streaming on Netflix.

While the new Resident Evil movie may be coming to home video on November 3, it's also staying in theaters. In fact, it was just announced that the movie is returning to IMAX and other premium large format (PLF) screens.

Cregger, who co-wrote and directed the new Resident Evil movie, recently discussed the backlash from the hardcore gamer community. He said he should have known better that fans of the games wouldn't embrace him and his ideas. After the movie came out and got great reviews and made tons of money, Cregger said he felt "gratified."

The filmmaker has said he has ideas for more Resident Evil movies, but he's not going to pursue them; instead, he's only going to make original, non-franchise movies going forward. His next movie, The Flood, is a sci-fi film starring Jennifer Lawrence.

title: Phantom Blade Zero Put Up Some Massive Sales Numbers
summary:
Developer S-Game's action-RPG Phantom Blade Zero launched on October 29 and had a massive start across PC and PS5.

The game sold more than 4 million copies over its first 72 hours. That works out to 926 units sold per minute or about 15.4 per second over the first three days.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the studio said in a social media post.

The 4 million figure counts copies sold across both PC and PS5--the game is not available on Xbox. The game reached a record of 833,921 peak concurrent users on Steam on November 1.

The game's developer is based in China, and the majority of preorders for the game came from China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.

Phantom Blade Zero's sales out of the gate are strong, but do not come close to another hit game from the Chinese game developer scene, Black Myth: Wukong. title: GTA 6 Buying Guide: Get Ready For Sticker Shock
summary:
Rockstar's GTA 6 finally releases on November 19, and if you're looking to play the game, you'll also need a console--and those are more expensive than ever. Here's a quick buying guide to help you understand what you need and how much the items will cost. 

A console

First, you'll need a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S console. The least expensive option for buying a new system outright is the Xbox Series S, which costs $500. Unfortunately, that's $200 more expensive than the system cost at launch in 2020--there are a number macroeconomic and AI factors that drove prices up significantly.

A new Xbox Series X, meanwhile, costs $750 for a system with no disc drive, or $800 for a console with a disc drive. GTA 6 is not available on a disc, but having a disc drive may still be important to you for other games and media like DVDs and Blu-rays. 

Switching to PlayStation, the least expensive system on Sony's side is the $600 digital edition, scaling up to $900 for a PS5 Pro (with a disc drive). PS5 Pro, as the most powerful of these options, is likely to provide the best experience from a technical and graphical standpoint, although the gameplay itself should be identical across all platforms.

These are all prices for brand-new units, but Sony offers certified refurbished PS5 consoles starting at $500. A certified refurbished Xbox Series S, meanwhile, goes for $400. These are the prices from Sony and Microsoft directly, but you can find secondhand consoles at a variety of other retailers, along with places like eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and Craigslist. As usual, check your local or preferred retailer to see the latest prices.

New and certified refurbished consoles come with everything you need--including the system, controller, and power cords. You will need a TV or monitor, but the odds are good that if you're looking to play GTA 6, you probably already have one. 

People on platforms outside PlayStation and Xbox are out of luck, as GTA 6 has not been announced for Switch 2 or PC. A PC edition is expected to release in early 2027, but there is no word on a Switch 2 version. 

The game

To play GTA 6 you will need to buy GTA 6. The game's standard edition goes for $80, with its Ultimate Edition selling for $100. As mentioned, the game is not available on a disc. That being said, retailers are selling the $80 edition in stores, though you only get a code in the box. The $100 edition appears to be exclusive to digital storefronts.

The $100 Ultimate Edition includes loads of extras, including a variety of cosmetics and even in-game shops that people who buy the $80 edition cannot access. Since GTA 6 is a digital-exclusive game, there is no reason to worry about units selling out, but if you do want to preorder, you get the Vintage Vice City Pack and a free month of GTA+.

GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013--adjusted for inflation, that's about $85 today.

You will also need an internet connection to install GTA 6, since it's a digital only game. It's a beefy one, too, weighing in at a reported 201GB. Thankfully, preloading begins on November 12, a full week before the game launches. That means you'll be able to begin downloading it early in the hopes of being ready to go on November 19.

November 12 is also when GTA 6's code-in-a-box copies will be available to buy at physical stores. You're not getting a week of early access, though, as the game does not unlock fully until November 19.

Do you need PS Plus or Game Pass?

GTA 6 is a strictly single-player game, and as such, you likely will not need PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass to play. Rockstar has yet to confirm this, however. 

Rockstar is surely going to release a new version of GTA Online at some point--some believe that will happen in early 2027. And at that point, you'll likely need a membership. But for launch, there is no online or multiplayer support, so we don't think a subscription to PS Plus or Game Pass would be required. 

Why no disc?

Neither Rockstar nor studio owner Take-Two have provided a reason for GTA 6 being a digital exclusive, but the answer seems pretty obvious: It's all about money. Rockstar makes more money from digital game sales, and having no disc eliminates the secondhand market. 

“A disc can be resold or rented a hundred times, and Rockstar earns nothing after that first sale," Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics said. 

The code-in-a-box strategy for physical games has been around for a long time already, and while people might complain online about the lack of a physical edition of GTA 6, the game is going to sell phenomenally no matter what, Mat Piscatella of Circana says.

Beyond these factors, consumer spending patterns have trended increasingly toward digital since the early 2010s. GTA 6 is such a large game in terms of its file size, so making it digital-exclusive also saves Rockstar and Take-Two money by not needing to print a second disc, if one was ever needed.

title: Resident Evil Requiem Drops To Lowest Price, But For One Day Only
summary:
Resident Evil Requiem is brilliant. I don’t need to tell you that—the critical scores across the board, feedback from both fans and newcomers, and the fact that Leon Kennedy returns are enough evidence to support my opinion. Halloween may be dead until next year, but what hasn’t died is the need to defeat hordes of infected. With the latest Resident Evil game cheaper than ever, there’s no better time to buy it. You only have one day to get it at this price, though.

What makes Resident Evil Requiem one of the best horror games and one of the best entries in the franchise is how it balances the recent first-person perspective entries with the survival horror-action hybrid of older games. As Grace Ashcroft, you’re forced to deal with enemies that will easily overpower you and, if you’re anything like me, avoid the darkness in that forsaken basement level. As Leon, it’s third-person horror and action, parrying fatal attacks with a satisfyingly timed hatchet block and unleashing a barrage of bullets against foes that you found horrifying as Grace.

Of course, the story follows a familiar Resident Evil plot, but it’s done so well that it remains captivating throughout. Grace’s story, as an FBI analyst, takes her to the hotel where her mother was murdered. Finally coming face-to-face with her trauma, she inevitably has to deal with a very clearly virus-infected researcher who wants her for some reason. You’ll have to find out why when you play it. Leon, an agent for the Division of Security Operations, has his own investigation, which eventually intertwines with Grace’s story, bringing everything together in a truly gripping way. As the meme suggests: absolute cinema.

I’m someone who has been a fan of both the old and new entries. I loved Resident Evil 2 and beyond, but I truly fell in love with the franchise with Resident Evil 7. Seeing both styles combined isn't confusing; it feels like the perfect blend. You’ll also get to play the new Leon Must Die Forever mode after completing the story. It's a time-based survival mode with roguelite elements, and alongside the usual Resident Evil speedrun shenanigans you may get up to, it really adds to your playtime.

Usually, you’d have to pay full price—or settle for a small discount—but right now, you can grab Resident Evil Requiem for just $40.59 / £34.79 at Fanatical, but only for 24 hours. That’s a Steam key, too, so you can add it to your library and start downloading it straight away. Or, you can add it to your backlog if you want. We’re all human after all. Well, except for the bioweapons, of course.

Spoiler alert: You’re in for a great time. After writing all this, I feel the urge to go backflip off a wall while dodging an attack for no reason. Weird.

title: Entire Games Are Being Ripped Off By AI, And Things Are Only Going To Get Worse
summary:
Popular video games have always attracted copycats, but the barrier--and timeline--for creating them has recently and suddenly been significantly lowered. The advent of generative AI and vibe-coding has made it nearly trivial for individuals with even light coding experience to pump out a fully formed copy of a popular game, or even an upcoming one. As a result, developers can have their ideas taken out from under them, siphoning money or enthusiasm for their own original ideas. 

The problem of easy copycats came to a head recently during Steam Next Fest, the platform's discoverability event that focuses on free demos of upcoming games. The recent Next Fest was awash with AI slop and even led some developers to consider abstaining from releasing demos.

To better understand the problem, GameSpot spoke with three developers, via email and direct messages, whose perspectives on the problem vary. But they agree that there's no clear path forward for studios to combat copycats, and change will need to come from platform holders themselves.

Rami Ismail is familiar with game clones. When his studio, Vlambeer, was preparing the release of mobile game Ridiculous Fishing in 2011, it was undercut by a clone called Ninja Fishing that beat it to the punch and made lots of money in the process, demoralizing the studio. Although that situation predates the AI vibe-coding era, the story of Vlambeer is a precursor to what we're seeing now. 

"It was devastating," Ismail said. "We had a firm belief that creativity was worthwhile, and the clone very quickly reminded us that ultimately, people with money will cynically steal anything they can. It was terrifying: We were firm believers in making the best possible games we could, and we were now reconsidering everything." 

Ismail said that today, in his conversations with other developers, there's a lot of uncertainty around marketing. 

"You either make a game slowly while building up a community, or you make something with a good hook quickly and hope it goes viral--in both cases, as soon as you gain momentum, you're easy prey for any asshole with a Claude account and $3,000 of tree-burning money," he said.

The problem of AI clones didn't exactly come out of left field for developers. While many in the hobbyist community are only learning about it recently, those with an ear to the ground have been seeing steady progress toward the current situation. Ismail said the conversation around AI has been swirling for a few years now, as the technology has progressed from a purely technical experiment and then moved into artistic pursuits like writing, art, and music. 

Mike Futter, director of operations and publishing at Causeway Studios and producer with Strange Scaffold, said that since derivative works have been a problem in the industry since before AI, it wasn't surprising that cloners quickly adopted the new technology.

"So while I hadn't heard about specific accusations or AI-enabled cloning until the wave of AI decompiling hit the mainstream recently (targeting major subscription software providers), it didn't surprise me one bit," Futter said. "And, because you can't protect game mechanics, we need platform support to protect developers."

Legal protections for games can include elements like art assets, sound, or narrative, but game mechanics themselves are much more difficult to copyright, especially when they're broad ideas or concepts. 

"When I hear about platforms turning a blind eye to AI slop that's worse than the shovelware of yesteryear, it deeply saddens me," Futter continued. "If platforms won't help create a firewall for developers, they should do it for the consumers clamoring for tools to weed out the slop."

Digital Sun, the studio that pulled back on its plans for a public demo for its upcoming game ReVamp, citing the danger of AI clones, said through a spokesperson that it had been watching other games struggle with clones or change plans based on the danger they present.

"[Needle in a Haystack Simulator] went viral on social media before it even had a Steam page, and now there are several identical clones of it," the studio said. "But what turned it into a real problem for us was Drunken Goddess Reflux. A game with over 500,000 wishlists was afraid to release a demo, when it should be exactly the opposite. Sure, a clone wouldn't have its wishlists, and probably not its incredible animation, either. But we don't know how fast the technology will keep advancing, or whether measures will be taken to protect original games. That uncertainty is what's pushing us to be cautious and change the way we connect with players, moving public builds closer to launch."

Needle in a Haystack Simulator is a major example of the problem, inspiring so many clones that the developer has cracked jokes about it. The game, which itself is something of a tongue-in-cheek joke based on the old idiom, challenges you to find a single needle in a pile of 5 million pieces of hay. That kind of simple viral concept is ripe for imitation. And Drunken Goddess Reflux developer Alliance Arts issued its own statement, pulling plans for a demo on October 16, days before Digital Sun followed suit. 

The developers we spoke to had differing opinions on their own use of AI. Ismail said developers tend to be curious about new technologies, so like many others, he's experimented with Large Language Models (LLMs) in a closed environment. Digital Sun said it has used AI as an assistive tool in development, but generates all of its own assets, and has firm guidelines on use of the technology. Futter said his studio, Causeway, is staunchly anti-AI and therefore does not use it for any experiments or assistance. 

For its part, Digital Sun moved its playtest from Steam to Discord. The studio said this allows it to limit who has access to its build of the game, with individual vetting for each user it grants access, and that helps reduce the possibility of clones. But logically, such a move comes at a cost. Public demos can be a major source of word-of-mouth buzz and even helpful metrics like Steam wishlists. Being forced to sacrifice that for fear of a slapdash AI clone hurts developers.

Futter said that, for the time being, developers will need to be prudent about what they share publicly and in demos. 

"Releasing demos is still important in 2026, but we have to be that much more careful about when and what we share publicly," he said. "One tip I learned from Brenda Romero when writing The GameDev Business Handbook is that developers should hold back at least one feature. Don't talk about it. Don't show it. Don't hint at it. And now, don't include anything about it in your public builds. Cloners (AI or otherwise) can't copy what they've never seen."

Ismail is more cynical about the situation. The threat of clones stealing the work of developers makes it hard to gain attention outside of the platforms that are already taking a big chunk of the sale price of each game sold. He said that the threat of clones, and studios being wary of releasing demos, "leaves developers with exactly zero ways of marketing their game that doesn't involve paying the ultra-rich even more money on top of the 30% they were already paying them. This outcome is a feature, not a bug."

Anthropic recently pushed out an update to the Claude Code prompt that seems aimed at stemming the tide of AI-generated clones, but how effective it will be, and if other AI models follow suit, remains to be seen.

For Valve's part, it has said it is aware of the problem of AI slop and looking into solutions. That statement was specifically in reference to the glut of AI slop that crowded the Next Fest charts, but naturally, better curation tools would help weed out low-effort clones as well. That said, Valve hasn't named any specific initiatives to address the problem, nor does it want to ban AI usage, and the developers widely agree that the solutions aren't clear. 

"[The solution] has to come from the platforms, ideally in conversation with developers, publishers and players," Digital Sun stated. "What does seem clear is that the current measures, like AI disclosures as they're set up today, aren't enough for a reality that has completely changed with the arrival of AI. These tools are evolving really fast, and we all need to find a way to keep up."

Ismail, similarly, was at a loss for an answer. 

"'Ban it' isn't going to work logistically, technically, or legally--no matter how much I'd love that," he said. "I think this is really going to be up to the developers and the audience on this one. I don't think we're getting a retry on AI, if they're successful--like F2P, it'll infect everything."

Futter, meanwhile, challenged platform holders like Steam to take their responsibility seriously, not just for the sake of players, but for the health of their own storefronts. If these stores become too inundated with AI slop and copycats, that will ultimately hurt their businesses, too. 

"It is not unreasonable to ask platforms to give us a simple tool to filter out AI slop," he said. "It is not an unreasonable ask for there to be penalties for not adhering to platform guidelines on AI disclosure. We know that the pushback against AI is working, because developers are hiding its use. We can already ignore titles one-by-one. We can weed out certain types of offerings, like adult-oriented games. Harsh penalties for failing to disclose are a matter of truth in advertising. If games are required to disclose use of AI on a store page (arguably one of the most powerful advertisements for a game), then failure to disclose amounts to deceptive marketing." 

However advanced and well-hidden AI copies get, though, Ismail said it will not be a substitute for the artistry of game development. The human touch comes from experience and fine-tuning, from play, and that's not something an LLM can replicate. 

"In 1979, an IBM training manual stated that, 'A computer can never be held accountable, therefore a computer must never make a management decision,'" he said. "A recent variant of that quote that stuck with me is that 'A computer can never be spiteful or horny, therefore a computer must never make art.' Having lived game development up close for decades, I believe game dev is not a scientific or technical job: The magic of game development exists in the messy, soft, human, confusing parts in between--the discussions between the programmer and artist that each see the world so differently but learned to communicate, the lines of dialogue that came from the pain of someone's recent breakup or the thrill of their recent crush, the fifth stubborn attempt at getting a mechanic just right despite everybody else having moved on."

The problem of AI clones didn't exactly come out of left field for developers. While many in the hobbyist community are only learning about it recently, those with an ear to the ground have been seeing steady progress toward the current situation. Ismail said the conversation around AI has been swirling for a few years now, as the technology has progressed from a purely technical experiment and then moved into artistic pursuits like writing, art, and music. 

Mike Futter, director of operations and publishing at Causeway Studios and producer with Strange Scaffold, said that since derivative works have been a problem in the industry since before AI, it wasn't surprising that cloners quickly adopted the new technology.

"So while I hadn't heard about specific accusations or AI-enabled cloning until the wave of AI decompiling hit the mainstream recently (targeting major subscription software providers), it didn't surprise me one bit," Futter said. "And, because you can't protect game mechanics, we need platform support to protect developers."

Legal protections for games can include elements like art assets, sound, or narrative, but game mechanics themselves are much more difficult to copyright, especially when they're broad ideas or concepts. 

"When I hear about platforms turning a blind eye to AI slop that's worse than the shovelware of yesteryear, it deeply saddens me," Futter continued. "If platforms won't help create a firewall for developers, they should do it for the consumers clamoring for tools to weed out the slop."

Digital Sun, the studio that pulled back on its plans for a public demo for its upcoming game ReVamp, citing the danger of AI clones, said through a spokesperson that it had been watching other games struggle with clones or change plans based on the danger they present.

"[Needle in a Haystack Simulator] went viral on social media before it even had a Steam page, and now there are several identical clones of it," the studio said. "But what turned it into a real problem for us was Drunken Goddess Reflux. A game with over 500,000 wishlists was afraid to release a demo, when it should be exactly the opposite. Sure, a clone wouldn't have its wishlists, and probably not its incredible animation, either. But we don't know how fast the technology will keep advancing, or whether measures will be taken to protect original games. That uncertainty is what's pushing us to be cautious and change the way we connect with players, moving public builds closer to launch."

Needle in a Haystack Simulator is a major example of the problem, inspiring so many clones that the developer has cracked jokes about it. The game, which itself is something of a tongue-in-cheek joke based on the old idiom, challenges you to find a single needle in a pile of 5 million pieces of hay. That kind of simple viral concept is ripe for imitation. And Drunken Goddess Reflux developer Alliance Arts issued its own statement, pulling plans for a demo on October 16, days before Digital Sun followed suit. 

The developers we spoke to had differing opinions on their own use of AI. Ismail said developers tend to be curious about new technologies, so like many others, he's experimented with Large Language Models (LLMs) in a closed environment. Digital Sun said it has used AI as an assistive tool in development, but generates all of its own assets, and has firm guidelines on use of the technology. Futter said his studio, Causeway, is staunchly anti-AI and therefore does not use it for any experiments or assistance. 

For its part, Digital Sun moved its playtest from Steam to Discord. The studio said this allows it to limit who has access to its build of the game, with individual vetting for each user it grants access, and that helps reduce the possibility of clones. But logically, such a move comes at a cost. Public demos can be a major source of word-of-mouth buzz and even helpful metrics like Steam wishlists. Being forced to sacrifice that for fear of a slapdash AI clone hurts developers.

Futter said that, for the time being, developers will need to be prudent about what they share publicly and in demos. 

"Releasing demos is still important in 2026, but we have to be that much more careful about when and what we share publicly," he said. "One tip I learned from Brenda Romero when writing The GameDev Business Handbook is that developers should hold back at least one feature. Don't talk about it. Don't show it. Don't hint at it. And now, don't include anything about it in your public builds. Cloners (AI or otherwise) can't copy what they've never seen."

Ismail is more cynical about the situation. The threat of clones stealing the work of developers makes it hard to gain attention outside of the platforms that are already taking a big chunk of the sale price of each game sold. He said that the threat of clones, and studios being wary of releasing demos, "leaves developers with exactly zero ways of marketing their game that doesn't involve paying the ultra-rich even more money on top of the 30% they were already paying them. This outcome is a feature, not a bug."

Anthropic recently pushed out an update to the Claude Code prompt that seems aimed at stemming the tide of AI-generated clones, but how effective it will be, and if other AI models follow suit, remains to be seen.

For Valve's part, it has said it is aware of the problem of AI slop and looking into solutions. That statement was specifically in reference to the glut of AI slop that crowded the Next Fest charts, but naturally, better curation tools would help weed out low-effort clones as well. That said, Valve hasn't named any specific initiatives to address the problem, nor does it want to ban AI usage, and the developers widely agree that the solutions aren't clear. 

"[The solution] has to come from the platforms, ideally in conversation with developers, publishers and players," Digital Sun stated. "What does seem clear is that the current measures, like AI disclosures as they're set up today, aren't enough for a reality that has completely changed with the arrival of AI. These tools are evolving really fast, and we all need to find a way to keep up."

Ismail, similarly, was at a loss for an answer. 

"'Ban it' isn't going to work logistically, technically, or legally--no matter how much I'd love that," he said. "I think this is really going to be up to the developers and the audience on this one. I don't think we're getting a retry on AI, if they're successful--like F2P, it'll infect everything."

Futter, meanwhile, challenged platform holders like Steam to take their responsibility seriously, not just for the sake of players, but for the health of their own storefronts. If these stores become too inundated with AI slop and copycats, that will ultimately hurt their businesses, too. 

"It is not unreasonable to ask platforms to give us a simple tool to filter out AI slop," he said. "It is not an unreasonable ask for there to be penalties for not adhering to platform guidelines on AI disclosure. We know that the pushback against AI is working, because developers are hiding its use. We can already ignore titles one-by-one. We can weed out certain types of offerings, like adult-oriented games. Harsh penalties for failing to disclose are a matter of truth in advertising. If games are required to disclose use of AI on a store page (arguably one of the most powerful advertisements for a game), then failure to disclose amounts to deceptive marketing." 

However advanced and well-hidden AI copies get, though, Ismail said it will not be a substitute for the artistry of game development. The human touch comes from experience and fine-tuning, from play, and that's not something an LLM can replicate. 

"In 1979, an IBM training manual stated that, 'A computer can never be held accountable, therefore a computer must never make a management decision,'" he said. "A recent variant of that quote that stuck with me is that 'A computer can never be spiteful or horny, therefore a computer must never make art.' Having lived game development up close for decades, I believe game dev is not a scientific or technical job: The magic of game development exists in the messy, soft, human, confusing parts in between--the discussions between the programmer and artist that each see the world so differently but learned to communicate, the lines of dialogue that came from the pain of someone's recent breakup or the thrill of their recent crush, the fifth stubborn attempt at getting a mechanic just right despite everybody else having moved on."
